Restructuring of APDRP 
t 241.    SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA:tf 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government has decided to launch a new Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP-II), after the failure of Accelerated Power 
Development and reforms Programme (APDRP); 
(b) if so, the targets proposed to be fixed thereunder; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the targets proposed under this programme have been 
declared unrealistic by the Planning Commission; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (d) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The Government had launched the Accelerated Power Development and Reforms 
Programme (APDRP) in the year 2002-03 with the objective of encouraging reforms, reducing 
Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) loss, improving quality of supply of power 
and improving consumer satisfaction. The target was to reduce AT&C losses to 15% in five 
years to begin with in urban and high density consumption areas. AT&C loss has come 
down in towns where APDRP has been implemented. Further, some of the utilities which 
adopted various interventions as envisaged under the programme have shown significant 
reduction in AT&C loss. At town level, AT&C losses have been brought below 20 per cent 
in 215 APDRP towns in the country of which 163 towns have brought AT&C losses below 
15 per cent. 
The Ministry of Power took up the evaluation of the programme through independent 
agencies. While recommending the continuance of the APDRP beyond Tenth Plan, the 
evaluators made certain suggestions for achieving better results. The State Power Utilities 
and the Planning Commission had also proposed certain modifications in the programme. 
Considering this, the Ministry of Power constituted a task Force, headed by Shri P. Abraham, 
former Secretary, Government of India, to assess and analyze the current efforts, suggestions 
made by various agencies and to suggest restructuring of the programme to achieve the 
objectives of APDRP. There have been discussions with the States thereafter. Keeping in 
view the recommendations/suggestions of the various stakeholders including State

Governments on the implementation of APDRP, and the desirability of having a result 
oriented programme, the programme is proposed to be restructured with revised terms and 
conditions during the Eleventh Five Year Plan to make it more effective. 
(b) It is proposed to introduce a restructured APDRP in the Eleventh Five Year Plan in 
selected project areas with focus on establishing baseline data of AT&C loss, sanctioning 
projects for improvement of distribution network and incentivising utilities which achieve 
the desired level of AT&C loss reduction. 
and (d) The revised proposal is being appraised in the Government.

*243. SHRI TARLOCHAN SINGH: Will th e Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that during his visit to Amritsar, the Prime Minister had made a 
public announcement for setting up of an institute of studies on Sri Guru Granth Sahib in 
that city; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that, for two years, various Department of the Ministry have 
held many meetings to finalize the project; 
(c) whether the land for this project was being given free by the Guru Nanak Dev 
University, Amritsar; 
(d) what is the fate of this project, which is lingering on for three year; and 
(e) whether the Prime Minister would honour his announcement? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN SINGH): (a) 
to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (e) On the occasion of the 400th Anniversary of the installation of Sri Guru Granth 
Sahib at the Golden Temple, the Prime Minister had announced that the Government of 
India would extend all possible help to set up a Centre of Research on Sri Guru Granth 
Sabhib in the Guru Nanak Dev University (GNDU), Amritsar Thereafter, the proposal of the 
GNDU for setting up of a National Institute of Studies in Sri Guru Granth Sahib (NISSGGS), 
Amritsar, as an autonomous body, was approved by the University Grants Commission 
(UGC) during X Plan Period. It was also decided by the UGC that the Expert Committee 
constituted by the UGC shall act as the Governing Body-cum-Advisory Committee to guide 

Oral Answers [17MARCH2008]. to Questions   9 
the affairs of the NISSGGS at GNDU, Amritsar till such time that the Governing Body was 
formally constituted. The above Expert Committee of UGC also recommended that the 
proposed Institute was to be funded entirely by UGC/MHRD on a permanent basis. An amount 
of Rs. 1.00 crore was also sanctioned through the UGC as seed money to GNDU, Amritsar. 
Besides, land for the Institute was also provided by the GNDU, Amritsar, free of cost. 
Subsequently, it was decided to establish the above Institute as an autonomous body under 
the MHRD and register it as a separate Society with the Registrar of Societies under the Societies 
Registration Act, 1860. However, later on, it was decided that instead of a new autonomous body, 
a Centre of Research on Sri Guru Granth Sahib Studies would be set up in the GNDU itself, which 
shall be fully funded by the MHRD through the UGC. Accordingly, a fresh proposal has been 
submitted by the GNDU, Amritsar to the UGC for the setting up of the Centre of Research on Sri 
Guru Granth Sahib. This is being evaluated by an Expert Committee of the UGC for finalizing the 
budgetary requirements for the entire XI Plan period. The necessary funds to the GNDU will be 
released for this purpose by the UGC.

DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the 
Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
• whether a high level committee had been set up, under the Chairmanship of Justice 
Shri Jasraj Chopra, to consider the demand of Gujjars, after the agitation for Gujjar reservation 
in Rajasthan; 
• whether the report of the Committee has been sent to the Central Government by the 
Rajasthan Government; 
• if so, the main recommendations of the Committee, alongwith the action being taken 
thereon; and 
• whether Justice Chopra has stated that th e norms for giving Schduled Tribe status 
are no longer applicable and are required to be reconsidered? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) to (d) A Statement is 
laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
• Yes, Sir. In view of persistent demand of the Gujjar community for 
inclusion in the notified list of Scheduled Tribes, the Government of Rajasthan 
has constituted a High Powered Committee headed by Justice (Retd.) Jasraj 
Chopra to examine the matter in detail and to submit its report. 
• A copy of the report of the High Powered Committee headed by Justice 
(Retd.) Jasraj Chopra has been sent to the Ministry of Tribal Affairs by the State 
Government of Rajasthan in December, 2007. 
• and (d) In its main recommendations the High Powered Committee has 
advised the Government of Rajasthan to (1) take the matter to the Government of 
India to abrogate the criteria used so far to include any class of people in the fold 
of Scheduled Tribes, as these have become obsolete and outdated. These should 
be replaced by quantifiable criteria that are relevant in the present context. The 
criteria should be such that they could stand judicial scrutiny and enable future 
Commissions or Committees appointed by the Government to examine the issue 
with exactitude and reliability; and 
(2) take immediate steps to set up a Board for Underdeveloped and Inconvenient Areas 
to attend to the problems faced by the people living a life of abject poverty in inaccessible, 
remote, and inconvenient areas such as ravines, Dangs and Chhinds, forests and hills— 
where development has not yet reached. These are the areas where most of the backward

the floor of the House by Shri Lalit Kishorc Chaturvedi.

amongst the Gujjars reside, and for whom th eir community leaders raised their voice. 
Development of such areas should not wait for the outcome of a classificatory exercise. For 
this purpose, the Government should benevolently allocate sizeable funds for a reasonable 
period of time by reprioritizing its developmental activities. Emphasis will have to be laid on 
(i) building roads to link these communities with the mainstream; (ii) motivating the children 
of these families to get educated; (iii) improving health and hygiene of the communities 
through provision of drinking water, immunization against major illnesses and better health 
care of children and of the aged. 
The High Powered Committee has also recommended that it would be desirable to provide 
all this in a special package, rather than to insert them in the already existing schemes. Also, 
this must be done with a sense of commitment and good zeal. The Government of Rajasthan 
is required to take action in terms of these recommendations.

ICDS in a mission mode 
*247. SHRIMATI SUPRIYASULE:tt 
SHRI JESUDASU SEELAM: 
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
• whether the Minister has declared that the Integrated Child Development Services 
Scheme has been put in a mission mode in the Eleventh Five Year Plan; 
• if so, whether Government was contemplating some kind of accreditation to NGOs 
and also ratings and incentives, to motivate them to do good work by 2020; 
• whether India would emerge as the youngest population in the world and the mandate 
for the Ministry was to prepare the nation to achieve excellence; and 
• if so, which other schemes, the Ministry is considering to improve the child plans in 
the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY):(a)to(d)AStatementislaidon 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) It is proposed to restructure the Integrated Child Development Services 
(ICDS) Scheme and implement it in a Mission Mode during the Eleventh Plan period. The 
details of the revamped Scheme are being worked out. 
(c) and (d) As per the Census of India 2011, the youth population in the age group of 
15-24 years is expected to increase to 240 million by 2011. The Ministry prepared a National 
Plan of Action for Children 2005. This Plan includes goals, objectives strategies and activities 
for improving nutritional status of children, reducing IMR and MMR, increasing enrolment 
ratio and reducing drop out rates, universalization of primary education, increasing coverage 
for immunization etc. The Plan also harmonized the goals for children set in the UN General 
Assembly Special Session on Children held in 2002 and the goals for children in related 
Ministries/Departments. 
Apart from ICDS, the other Schemes of the Ministry for the benefit of children include 
Rajiv Gandhi National Creche Scheme for the children of working mothers, Grant-in-aid 
scheme for voluntary organizations, Scheme for Welfare of Working Children in Need of 
Care and Protection, Central Adoption Resource Agency and Juvenile Justice (Care and 
Protection of Children) Act, 2000.

Government school students going for tuitions 
1747. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJM A A. HEPTULLA: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 whether Government is aware that students of Government schools go for tuitions 
more than those in private schools; 
 if so, whether education imparted in Government schools is not up to the mark; and 
 whether this also defeats the goal of Government for providing free and fair education 
to all children across the board? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) Education is a concurrent 
subject and school education primarily comes under the purview of the State 
Governments. Government of India is not aware of any findings establishing that 
students of Government schools go for tuitions more than those in private schools. So far 
as the schools under this Ministry are concer ned, there is no evidence to suggest that 
education imparted in these schools is not up to the mark. On the contrary, pass 
percentages in schools under Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan and Navodaya Vidyalaya 
Samiti, both at class X and XII, were consistently above the pass percentages in 
independent private schools affiliated to Ce ntral Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) 
during the last five years (2003-07). 
(c) No, Sir. Education in Government schools up to the elementary stage is already free. 
Central Government has been implementing Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) at the elementary 
level since 2001-02, inter-alia, with the objective to achieve universal elementary education 
by 2010 and to improve quality in Government schools. It has also been decided to implement 
a centrally sponsored scheme for universalisation of access to and improvement of quality 
of education at the secondary stage during the Eleventh Five Year Plan.

Drop-out rate      
1756. SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that there is 14.4 per cent drop-out rate in grade I and 4.4 per cent 
in grades II and HI; 
 if so, the reasons for these drop-outs especially when the primary level education is 
free and mostly supported by Mid-day Meals; 
 whether it is due to non-availability of teachers, especially in rural areas and creaky 
infrastructure; and 
 the steps adopted by Government to ensure zero-tolerance level relating to drop-outs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) During 2004-05, drop-out rate at primary stage 
(Classes I-V) was 29 per cent. Grade wise drop-out rate are not being calculated. 
(b) to (d) The socio-economic and school related factors affect drop-outs. A multi-
pronged approach has been adopted under the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) for reducing 
drop-out rates. These include, inter alia, strengthening of schools and improving the 
quality of education through improvement in school infrastructure, recruitment of additional 
teachers, provision, provision of annual school grants, regular training of teachers, regular 
academic support to teachers etc. In addition, interventions under SSA also aim at building 
community support, flexible schooling for the hardest to reach children, special provision 
to promote education of girls, as well as children with special need. The Mid-day Meal 
programme also complements the strategy to reduce dropout rates.

Universities in the country 
1758. SHRI GANDHI AZAD: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
 the total number of universities functioning, as on date, under Central/State 
Governments all over the country; 
 the post-wise/grade-wise readers, professors, lecturers and others appointed in these 
universities, alongwith number of SCs and STs appointed; 
 whether there is any SC/ST backlog in these universities; 
 if so, the details thereof and since when the backlog exists; 
 whether any action has been taken to fill up such backlog; 
 if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
 by when the backlog vacancies of all cadre would be filled up? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRYOF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) According to the University Grants Commission 
(UGC), there are 419 Universities/Deemed-to-be Universities/Institutes of National 
Importance/Institutes established under State Legislation existing as on 11.03.2008. Out of 
these 25 are Central Universities and 233 are State Universities. 
(b) to (d) The information is being collected and will be laid on the Table of the House. 
(e) to (g) The University Grants Commission has formulated Guidelines for strict 
observation of Reservation Policy of the Government in Universities, Deemed-to-be 
Universities, Colleges and other Grant-In-Aid Institutions and Centres in 2006 and have 
sent the same to all Universities including those under the Central and State Governments 
for implementation. Universities have also been instructed by the UGC to fill up the backlog 
vacancies before filling any general Vacancy and those on adhoc basis. However, no definite 
time-frame can be given with regard to completely filling up the backlog.

Judicial reforms 
1762. SHRI AMIR ALAM KHAN: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to

Written Answers to [17 MARCH 2008] Unstarred Questions   83 
 if so, the details thereof; and 
 by when these are likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) to (c) Judicial 
reforms is a continuous process. It has to keep pace with the changing time, conditions and 
requirements of the people. Government is committed to providing speedy and inexpensive 
justice to the common man. 
Various judicial reform measures being implemented by the Government include: Scheme 
of Fast Track Courts and Family Courts, Infrastructure support for Judiciary including 
computerization, simplification of judicial procedures, augmenting Judges strength in High 
Courts, training of Judicial Officers for improvement in the quality of administration of 
justice, accountability of judges, organizing Lok Adalats and encouraging alternative modes 
of dispute resolution, setting up of special tribunals etc. Further, with a view to providing 
speedy, affordable and substantive justice to the poor at the grassroots level, the Government 
has introduced the Gram Nyayalaya Bill, 2007 in the Parliament. 
Selection of Judges 
1763. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be 
pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that political affiliation, besides judicial calibre is a factor in the 
appointment of Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts, as told by Government to an 
applicam under the RTI Act and also reported in the media; 
 if so, the details of cases in which Government holds back names of Judges, as 
contained in official reply of Government; 
 whether Government is planning to make selection process of Judges of High Courts 
and Supreme Court transparent; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ). (a) and (b) Pursuant 
to the Supreme Court Judgment of October 6, 1993 read with their Advisory Opinion of 
October 28, 1998, the process of initiation of proposal for appointment of Judges of the 
Supreme Court lies with the Chief Justice of India and for the High Court, it lies with the 
Chief Justice of that High Court. 
As per the Memorandum of Procedure for appointment of Judges drawn on the basis of 
the said judgment, Judges are selected keeping in view their educational qualifications, 
nature and extent of practice, length of the practice, the field of specialisation and professional 
income for the last three years. Besides this , the competence of the person, his judicial 
potential, temperament and integrity are also kept in mind. All this information, as also other 
background information including regarding political affiliations/leanings of the recommendee 
persons are made available to the Chief Jus tice of India for consideration by the Supreme 
Court Collegium. It is the Collegium which considers all the available information on the 
candidates and forms a view regarding their suitability or otherwise for appointment as 
Judges of the Supreme Court/High Courts. As per the above judgment of the Supreme 
Court, the responsibility for selection of candidates for appointment as Judges of Supreme 
Court and the High Courts lies with the judiciary.

change in the present system of appointment of Judges in the Supreme Court and the High

the last three years, and how it compares with that in other developed countries; and 
 what has been done to expand and upgrade Transmission and Distribution of electricity? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) In the earlier 
system of monitoring, utilities used to monitor Transmission and Distribution (T&D) losses. T&D 
losses were being computed taking into account electricity bills issued to consumers as accrued 
income and not on actual collection basis. T&D losses for the years 2003-04,2004-05 and 2005-06 
were 32.53%, 31.25% and 30.42% respectively of the total energy available for sale. In that 
system there was a tendency of utilities b ooking distribution losses under subsidized/un-
metered supply, thereby under reporting the former. The concept of Aggregate

Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses was introduced in the year 2001-02. AT&C loss 
captures not only technical losses, but also th eft, pilferages and commercial losses due to 
poor metering and billing and due to non-realisation of dues. The draft report on Performance 
of State Power Utilities for the years 2004-05 to 2006-07 prepared by the Power Finance 
Corporation indicates that the Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) Losses of the 
State Power Utilities at the national level for 2004-05,2005-06 and 2006-07 was 34.33%, 34.54% 
and 32.07% respectively of the total energy available for sale. T&D losses in some of the

distribution segments rests with the States. However, the Central Government had launched the

1799. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that Transmission and Distribution (T&D) losses have been rising 
alarmingly; 
 if so, the details thereof, along with the reasons therefor; 
 whether Government proposes to introduce some new technology to minimize the 
Transmission and Distribution losses; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) The draft 
report on Performance of State Power Utilities for the years 2004-05 to 2006-07 prepared 
by the Power Finance Corporation indica tes that the Aggregate Technical and 
Commercial (AT&C) losses [which includes Transmission and Distribution (T&D) losses 
also] of the State Power Utilities at the national level for 2004-05,2005-06 and 2006-07 
were 34.33%, 34.54% and 32.07% respectively of the total energy available for sale. 
There has been an arrest in the increase of AT&C losses in the country. The reasons for 
losses include technical reasons such as ov erloading of existing lines and substation 
equipment, old and outdated network, low HT: LT ratio, poor repair and maintenance of 
equipment, non installation of sufficient capacitors, substandard, inefficient and poor 
quality distribution equipment, poor power factor of consumer end devices etc. as also 
commercial reasons such as defective meters, theft and pilferage, tampering of meters, 
low accountability of employees, poor metering efficiency, poor billing efficiency, non 
realization of dues etc. 
(c) and (d) It is proposed to introduce a restructure Accelerated Power Development 
and Reforms Programme (APDRP) in the Eleventh Five Year Plan with focus on establishing 
baseline data of AT&C loss and IT enabled automated energy accounting systems, IT

enabled consumer service centres, and on projects for improvement of distribution 
networks.

11803. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJ1THA: 
SHR1 RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programmes 
(APDRP) was planned in 2003 for extensive reforms in power sector; 
 whether the target of bringing down Transmission and Distribution (T&D) losses of 
power upto fifteen per cent during the next five years was fixed under the programme; 
(c) if so, the facts thereof and the progress made in the direction of achieving the 
stipulated targets in the country upto December, 2007; and 
(d) the state of T&D losses of power during 2006-07? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) Government had 
launced Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) in the year 
2002-03 with the objective of encouraging reforms and of reduction in Aggregate Technical 
and Commercial (AT&C) loss, improving qua lity of supply of power and improving 
consumer satisfaction. 
 The target under APDRP was to reduce AT&C losses to 15% in five years to begin 
with in urban and high density consumption areas. 
 AT&C loss has come down in towns where APDRP has been implemented. Further, 
some of the utilities which adopted various interventions as envisaged under the programme 
have shown significant reduction in AT&C loss. At town level, AT&C losses have been 
brought below 20 per cent in 215 APDRP towns in the country of which 163 towns have 
brought AT&C losses below 15 per cent. 
 The draft report on Performance of Stat e Power Utilities for the years 2004-05 to 
2006-07 prepared by the Power Finance Corporation indicates that the Aggregate Technical 
and Commercial (AT&C) loss of the State Power Utilities at the national level for 2006-07 
was 32.07% of the total energy available for sale.

existing policy.

benefits are available:— 
(i) Zero Customs Duty: Import of capital equipment free of customs duty in terms

(Department of Revenue) read together with Notification No. 49/2006-Customs

 whether the Ministry has recently advised the power generating PSUs and other 
allied undertakings, to accord desired importance to the training of their workforce.to

should allocate adequate funds to training and development activities for meeting the 
stipulated training requirements. 
The various power generation PSUs like NTPC Ltd., National Hydroelectric Power 
Corporation Ltd. (NHPC), Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam Ltd. (SJVNL), Tehri Hydro Development

Employees engaged in generation and maintenance of power plants are also being

breakdowns/outages thereby giving a far better plant performance leading to a higher

power plants in the country during the current financial year (April, 2007-Febr-uary, 2008)

number factors like installed capacity, age of the units, past performance, planned outages,

monsoon and non-monsoon season as well as irrigation requirements influence performance 
of hydro-power stations, the quality and availability of fuel have a bearing on the 
performance of thermal power stations. Therefore, the actual performance of some power 
plants, mostly in the state sector, is at variance with their normal working capacity. 
(d) The following steps have been/are being taken by the Government of India to bring 
improvement in the generation capacity of poorly performing stations:

administrative function.

The UPA administration will take all measures to reconcile the objectives of economic

on forests are concerned.

will be discontinued. Cooperation of these communities will be sought for protecting forests

to cultivate forest land to the extent under occupation, the right to own, collect, use and 
dispose of minor forest produce, rights inside forests like grazing etc. which are traditional 
and customary. The Act enjoins upon these beneficiaries the duties for protecting wild life, 
forest and their bio-diversity also.

Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored Sector for the welfare and upliftment of Scheduled 
Tribes and for the development of the areas where Scheduled Tribes reside.

Illegitimate new born babies 
1860. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will th e Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that many illegitimate new born babies are found thrown and 
abandoned in garbage, etc. and some of them are adopted by the needy couples; 
 if so, the details of such cases/incidents during 2006 and 2007 and the number of 
infants among them, who have dies for want of proper care; 
 how the survived babies, not adopted by any one, are brought up the nurtured; and 
 the steps being taken to prevent tendency to abandoned such infants? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT(SHRIMATIRENUKACHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) No, Sir. This Ministry 
has no such information. However, legal adoption of orphan, abandoned and surrendered 
children is carried out by recognized adoption agencies all over the country. 
 The orphan, abandoned and surrendered babies, if not adopted, are kept under 
institutional care in children's homes or given in foster care as per the Juvenile Justice (Care 
and Protection of Children) Act, 2000 and its Amendment Act, 2006. 
 Ministry of Women and Child Development has formulated a new centrally sponsored 
scheme namely 'Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS)' for implementation during 11th 
Plan period under which there is provision for setting up of Cradle Baby Reception Centres 
in each district. These Cradle Baby Reception Centres will be linked to Cradle Points at 
Primary Health Care Centres (PHCs), Hospitals/Nursing Homes, Swadhar Units, Short Stay 
Homes and in the office of the District Child Protection Unit to receive abandoned babies. 
For every child received by the cradle baby reception centre, the process of creating an 
individual care plan shall be initiated by the reception centre, to be further developed and 
prepared by the Specialized Adoption Agency (SAA) in whos e care the child is to be 
transferred after the authorization of the Child Welfare Committee (CWC). 
Efforts have been made by the Central Adoption Resource Agency (CARA) and its 
associated agencies and the State Governments to prevent abandonment of infants through 
various publicity and awareness campaign, etc.

Demand for Removal of Restriction on Sale of Wheat by Farmers of 
Punjab and Haryana 
SHRI TARLOCHAN SINGH (HARYANA): Sir, recently a news item appeared in newspapers 
in Punjab and Haryana that the Government of India was adopting a new policy of not 
allowing the fanners to sell their wheat to anyone other than the FCI and other Government 
procuring agencies. Sir, Punjab and Haryana contribute more than 80 per cent of the wheat to 
the national kitty. Now, when the produce comes, the farmers want to have more money. You 
allow traders to sell anywhere in India, but the poor farmers of Haryana and Punjab are not 
allowed to sell their crops outside. You are putting a restriction on them. Even on storage of 
wheat, there is a restriction. So, our plea is that on the one side, you say that you are helping 
the farmers. But when the farmers get a chance to get more money above the market price, 
above the procurement price, then, the Government intervenes and stops it. Today, the market 
price of wheat is Rs. 1,200 per quintal. But you have fixed the price at Rs. 1,000 per quintal. 
And, the cost of wheat is Rs. 1,250 per tonne, and you import it at Rs. 1,600 per tonne. But now, 
when farmers of Punjab and Haryana are coming forward and the production of crops this time 
is not very good due to bad we ather conditions, I request the Government not to put any 
restriction on sale by Punjab and Haryana farmers. They should have freedom and full access 
to the private market. The Government should not interfere and do anything against their 
interests; otherwise, if the farmer is not given remunerative prices and he is not able to earn 
profit, he would remain in debt and every time a demand would be raised to waive off his loans. 
So, this is the time to help farmers in Punjab and Haryana.

MISS PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, in th e present time, in view of large-scale 
unemployment of the educated youths, it is felt imperative that our National Education 
Policy is revitalised. In the past, several Committees and Commissions were set up to go into the 

Special [17 MARCH 2008] Mentions    189 
issue of unemployment of uneducated youths, and views have been expressed that vocational 
training to students at secondary schools level will go a long way to solve the problem. Many 
of the students, not being able to pursue higher studies, leave the schools and go in search of 
jobs. But, without a vocational training background, they remain unemployed. And, unemployment 
tempts them to commit crime and voilence, leading to social disorder. 
I would urge upon the Government that it is high time that we reframed our National 
Education Policy. Imparting vocational training at the Secondary Schools level should be 
made mandatory, and India being predominantly an agricultural country, training on 
agricultural land and other allied trade should be undertaken. Instructors on different trades 
should be appointed to impart both theoretic and practical training and they should be 
allotted area for practical purpo ses. This alone can tide ov er the present unemployment 
crisis of a large number of educated youths.

Demand to Provide 'Health for All' 
SHRI MOINUL HASSAN (West Bengal): Sir, 'Health for All' as a fundamental right was the 
declaration of the Alma Ata World Conference. To achieve this goal, it is necessary to take 
social and economic steps. So many assurances were given in the food policy but this remains 
on paper only. Sir, every seven minutes, a woman dies due to pregnancy-related complications. 
Every half-an-hour, 50 children under five-years of age die. All this could have been avoided, 
had the problem been addressed adequately and early. A poor country like India must take 
preventive measures which, in turn, can save public money. The first preventive measure is 
adequate intake of food. Inadequate food intake amongst people, particularly amongst women 
and children, causes various diseases forcing them to go in for medical treatment. 
Sir, in such a situation, the private drug industry has got involved in a conspiracy to disrupt 
the price control measures of the Government in league with some officials. As a result, prices 
of drugs have shot up by leaps and bounds which has hit the poor severely. The private and big 
multinational drug companies are increasing prices of drugs and building big hospitals. Poor 
Government hospitals do not match their infrastructure. So, the Alma Ata Conference had 
adopted the goal of'Health for All' but in India under the new economic and liberalisation policy the 
Government has been withdrawing its intervention in the health sector, thus, leaving the helpless 
people to the private sector sharks. Therefore, the Government should come forward to honour 
its commitment made through the Alma Ata declaration and strictly control the prices of 
drugs.

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I am

over a five years' time period as well as over a one year's time period. There is a vast diference

not only in the rate of growth that we have experienced over the last four years, there is a very 
significant and important difference in the overall financial health of the country. If you look at 
the growth rate between 1991-92 and 1997-98, growth averaged barely 6 per cent except for three 
years the growth was well below 6 per cent. Between 1998-99 and 2003-04, which can be taken 
as a reference period, average growth rate was 5.9 per cent. In fact, in two of those six years 
growth was less than 4.5 per cent but the overall average was about 5.9 per cent. In the three full 
years of the UPA Government and if you add the fourth year, which is coming to an end in about 
a fortnight from today, the growth has averaged close to 8.7 but with some luck it might be even 8.8 
per cent. 
Sir, this is simply not an increase of about 290 basis points. This means that the Indian 
economy has moved on to a higher growth plane and that responsibility on the Government

Sir, I was somewhat disappointed that a number of commentators did not grasp the 
significance of keeping the fiscal deficit, next year, below 3 percent. I am allowed 3 per cent, 
but I have deliberately kept it at 2.5 per cent. 1 wish to take a minute to explain this. We live 
in an uncertain world. We live in a world where there is considerable financial turbulence. 
Commodity prices and food prices are rising everyday. And, presently, I will show what the 
figures are. We have some liabilities that have not yet been quantified, for example, the Sixth 
Central Pay Commission. We have taken on, in 2008-09, a very large liability in terms of 
funding the loan waiver for farmers. Having regard to all this, we thought it was prudent that 
we peg the fiscal deficit at 2.5 per cent, leaving us some headroom, just in case it may be 
necessary to borrow that amount. Fiscal deficit is equal to borrowing. By leaving a headroom 
of 0.5 per cent of the GDP, we have allowed ourselves some flexibility in meeting, both, 
anticipated and unanticipated liabilities so that at the end of the year we still remain well

described this Budget as a communal Budget. 1 do not understand what a communal Budget 
is. I think, Sir, prejudice is really deep-seated in certain hearts and certain minds. When we 
provide scholarships, we prov ide scholarships to children, and, when a child receives a 
scholarship, I do not see a Hindu child, a Muslim child, a Christian child or a Sikh child; we

lesser opportunities, some children have lesser access, why should we not lean in favour of 
those children? Do we not all ag ree that there is a gender gap, and, therefore, we lean in 
favour of the girl child? Do we not acknowledge that as there is a gender inequality, therefore,

there is a caste gap between the so-called forward communities and OBCs, programmes are 
designed leaning in favour of OBC. When we find that there is a large caste gap through 
centuries of discrimination, do we not design programmes that lean in favour of Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes? So, when we find that there is a gap between the non-
minority communities, that is, the majority community, and, the minority communities in 
matters of education, access to scholarship, I ask myself, what is wrong if the Government 
leans in favour of the minority communities and designs programmes that are targeted for 
the minority communities. I think, this perfectly right. This is what any civilized nation 
should do, and, this is precisely what this Government is doing. If you want to call it a 
communal Budget, please do so but really you are exposing the prejudices that are deep 
seated in your hearts and minds. We reject these prejudices; we do not share these prejudices.

money in consumers' pockets, fiscal measures to reduce the cost, at least, the tax cost to the

work and the economy will continue to grow at a high rate in 2008-09

coalition Government last year there is no popular Government in office today. Therefore, 
the Budget takes on an important responsibility of ensuring that the growth and development

growth has tapered off in the State subsequently to 7.5 in subsequent years. Sir, the increased 
Plan Outlays, and the increased allocations in the Budget to the various sectos are welcome 
and on behalf of the people of Karnataka I thank the Government for the same.

my State to make kannada a classical language and for renaming its cities to be more 
reflective of their historical identities and cu lture. Both these are pending with the Union 
Government and I would urge the Government through the Finance Minister to expeditiously 
clear the same.

generates considerable direct and indirect taxes from our city and Bengaluru is as much a 
city of India as it is a city of Karnataka. I am disappointed that the Budget and Statement do

particular. Sir, would urge the Government through the Finance Minister that Bengaluru 
must be treated as a strategic city just as Mumbai has been and I would urge for a complete 
package for infrastructure and urban development to make it a modern metropolis. The 
current and unnecessary controversy of closing down an existing airport points to the lack 
of a coherent vision for infrastructure development and capacity development in our city.

gives it at five per cent. So, all the States, in the part of the country, are giving agricultural loans 
at very low rates. But there is a small history to it and I thought I should mention this history 
before we understand this statement in perspective. Sir, N ABARD provides refinance at 2.5 per 
cent. It is because N ABARD is providing refinance at 2.5 per cent that cooperative societies are 
able to lend at a lower rate. When the NDA was in office, agricultural loans were given at 10 per 
cent. In their last year of office, they reduced it to 9 per cent. When we came to office, in the first 
year, I reduced it to 9 per cent and implemented that 9 per cent. Next year, we reduced it to 7 per 
cent and now; all loans, not only of cooperative institutions, but also public sector banks and 
RRBs, are given at 7 per cent. So, the starting point is 7 per cent. Subsidy up to 7 per cent is borne 
by the Central Government. Beyond 7 per cent, it is the State Government that is providing 
additional subsidy—Tamil Nadu provides 2 per cent, Karnataka provides a subsidy, Andhra 
Pradesh provides a subsidy, Orissa provides a subsidy—which is the reason why they are able 
to lend at 5 per cent. But the two important things, which Mr. Venkaiah Naidu did not mention, 
were, one that the Central Government provides a subsidy of 2 per cent, and two, that N ABARD 
refinances at 2.5 per cent. These two factors in addition to the State Government's contribution 
of subsidy are the reason why it is able to provide loans at 4 per cent. So, we are playing our part 
and the State Governments are playing their part. That is how the farmer is getting loans at 4 per 
cent. I don't take away credit from the State Governments but I ask you humbly to give credit to 
the Central Government and NABARD also.
